This BitMat package should be massive for the new era of 1bit-LLM - substantially reducing the memory footprint of LLMs![Image 1: 🔥](https://abs.twimg.com/emoji/v2/svg/1f525.svg) Utilizes highly optimized kernels for matrix multiplication, tailored for performance and efficiency. ![Image 2: 📌](https://abs.twimg.com/emoji/v2/svg/1f4cc.svg) Its designed to optimize matrix multiplication operations by utilizing custom kernels written in Triton. The package leverages the principles outlined in the "1bit-LLM Era" paper, specifically utilizing packed int8 data to enhance computational efficiency and performance in deep learning and numerical computing tasks. ---- ![Image 3: 📌](https://abs.twimg.com/emoji/v2/svg/1f4cc.svg) Once you load a model with BitMat, the model operates in two distinct modes: ![Image 4: 👉](https://abs.twimg.com/emoji/v2/svg/1f449.svg) Evaluation Mode: By default, the model employs quantized weights, optimizing performance for inference tasks. Activate this mode using model.eval(). ![Image 5: 👉](https://abs.twimg.com/emoji/v2/svg/1f449.svg) Training Mode: Switching to this mode, via model.train(), allows the model to leverage full-precision weights, which is essential for training and fine-tuning processes, ensuring accurate gradient calculations and effective model updates. --- ![Image 6: 📌](https://abs.twimg.com/emoji/v2/svg/1f4cc.svg) The core insight from the "1bit-LLM Era" paper is that the precision of model parameters can be effectively reduced to 1.58 bits, meaning that all model parameters can assume values of -1, 0, or 1. To leverage this finding, they have developed a specialized Triton kernel to handle both training and inference processes efficiently. ![Image 7: 📌](https://abs.twimg.com/emoji/v2/svg/1f4cc.svg) During the training phase, they implement a custom forward and backward propagation mechanism that calculates the gradient as outlined in the paper. This is done in FP16 precision using the pre-quantized weights (W) and inputs (X). ![Image 8: 📌](https://abs.twimg.com/emoji/v2/svg/1f4cc.svg) For inference, the package optimized storage by packing the model weights into int8 format, achieving a 4x reduction in size. Its kernels then unpack these values during computation, perform the necessary multiplications, and accumulate the results. This approach significantly reduces the memory footprint required for storing and operating the model. ------ Its expected roughly 50% VRAM savings (if not more), since their repo includes code for int8 latent quantization (instead of the typical fp16) and int2(packed) weights instead of the typical Q_4/Q_5 quants that are common right now.
[![Image 9: https://github.com/astramind-ai/BitMat](https://pbs.twimg.com/media/GKQ6NcnWQAAvkz4?format=jpg&name=small)](https://x.com/rohanpaul_ai/status/1775608234180558851/photo/1)
